title: Design a Ride-Sharing System (like Uber/Ola): location tracking (GPS), matching driver to rider (geospatial index), ETA calculation, surge pricing, trip state machine.
keyPoints: Drivers send GPS coordinates every few seconds; a geospatial index (geohash, Redis GEO) enables fast nearby-driver queries.
Matching picks the nearest available driver by shortest ETA, with an atomic claim to prevent double-assignment.
ETA uses a routing engine over the road network with live traffic, not straight-line distance.
Surge pricing multiplies the fare based on the ratio of open requests to available drivers in an area.
A strict trip state machine (REQUESTED -> MATCHED -> ARRIVED -> IN_PROGRESS -> COMPLETED) prevents illegal transitions.
The driver claim must be atomic so one driver is never offered to two riders simultaneously.
Location data is best-effort (tolerate missed pings), but matching and billing require strict correctness.

s1_definition.oneliner: Index driver locations geospatially for fast nearest-driver matching, estimate arrival with routing, price by live supply and demand, and move every trip through a strict state machine.
s1_definition.profdef:
- **Geospatial index** : encodes locations for fast nearby queries (geohash, Redis GEO commands).
- **Driver matching** : picks the best available driver by shortest ETA with an atomic claim.
- **Surge pricing** : dynamic fare multiplier based on the ratio of open requests to available drivers.
- **Trip state machine** : enforces legal transitions (REQUESTED -> MATCHED -> ARRIVED -> IN_PROGRESS -> COMPLETED).
- **Atomic claim** : marks a driver as busy in one indivisible operation so two riders cannot be promised the same car.
s1_definition.analogy: National Bank of India runs a fleet of cash-delivery vans. The dispatch system always knows where every van is on a live map, finds the closest free van, tells the branch it will arrive in eight minutes, charges more when every van is busy during a rush, and tracks the delivery through stages. Replace vans with cars and branches with riders.

sections.s3_flow:
```text
  Ride-Sharing Architecture

  ┌──────────┐  GPS every 3s  ┌──────────────┐
  │ Driver   │───────────────►│ Geo Index    │
  │ App      │                │ (Redis GEO)  │
  └──────────┘                └──────┬───────┘
                                     │ nearby query
  ┌──────────┐  ride request  ┌──────▼───────┐
  │ Rider    │───────────────►│ Matching     │
  │ App      │                │ Service      │
  └──────────┘                │ (atomic claim│
                              │  on driver)  │
                              └──────┬───────┘
                                     │
  Trip State Machine:
  REQUESTED ──► MATCHED ──► ARRIVED ──► IN_PROGRESS ──► COMPLETED
       │            │                                       │
       └── CANCELLED └── CANCELLED                    Payment + Rating

  Surge pricing:
  open_requests / available_drivers = ratio
  ratio <= 1.0 -> 1.0x (no surge)
  ratio  > 1.0 -> min(3.0, 1 + ratio - 1) surge
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
A ride-sharing system is real-time and location-heavy, built around geospatial indexing, atomic driver matching, routing-based ETA, surge pricing, and a strict trip state machine. The atomic driver claim is the correctness linchpin: one driver must never be offered to two riders.

Location data is best-effort (tolerate missed pings), but matching and billing demand strict correctness. Separating these concerns is what keeps the platform both responsive and trustworthy.

Remember one sentence: index driver locations geospatially, match with an atomic claim, price by live supply-demand ratio, and enforce a strict trip state machine from request to completion.
